value.overview: The Maguari Stork (Ciconia maguari) is a large South American stork associated mainly with open wetlands and seasonally flooded grasslands. It is the only New World member of the genus Ciconia and one of three native storks found in the Americas. Its broad white wings and body contrast with black flight feathers, while its long legs and bill are adapted for wading and capturing prey in shallow water.
value.classification: The Maguari Stork belongs to the stork family Ciconiidae and the order Ciconiiformes. Its scientific name is Ciconia maguari.
value.identification: A large, long-legged stork with mostly white plumage, black flight feathers, a black bill, and reddish or pinkish legs. Adults have a dark facial area around the eye and a distinctive black tail and wing pattern visible in flight. The species is similar to the Wood Stork and Jabiru, but the Maguari Stork has a straighter, more pointed bill, a slimmer appearance, and less extensive black on the head and neck. Juveniles are duller and often show darker legs and bill.
value.rangeHabitat: The Maguari Stork occurs mainly east of the Andes, from Venezuela and eastern Colombia through the Guianas, Bolivia, Paraguay, Brazil, Uruguay, and Argentina. It uses open lowland habitats such as freshwater marshes, flooded savannas, shallow lagoons, mudflats, wet grasslands, rice fields, and seasonally flooded agricultural areas, generally avoiding dense forest. In Costa Rica it is an accidental or extremely rare vagrant, with documented occurrence near the Gulf of Nicoya, including the Chomes area; it is not a regular resident.
value.migrationStatus: Movement patterns are not fully understood, but the species makes seasonal movements linked to rainfall, flooding, and food availability. Some populations form large dry-season or nonbreeding aggregations. In Costa Rica, it is not a regular migrant or breeding species; records represent rare wandering individuals, including a documented occurrence near Chomes on the Gulf of Nicoya.
value.breeding: Breeding is associated with seasonal rains and shallow freshwater wetlands. Pairs may form or reunite in gatherings before nesting, and the species can breed colonially. In much of Brazil and Argentina, nests are large platforms of reeds and other wetland vegetation built on the ground or above shallow water, although shrubs may be used in parts of the northern range. Clutches commonly contain about three or four eggs. There is no reliable evidence of breeding in Costa Rica.
value.dietFeeding: The Maguari Stork is an opportunistic carnivore that feeds in shallow water and wet grassland. Its prey includes fish, eels, frogs, tadpoles, aquatic invertebrates, crustaceans, snakes, small reptiles, earthworms, insects, and small mammals such as rodents. It usually hunts visually, walking slowly with its bill near the water surface, but may also probe muddy bottoms. Outside the breeding season, it can forage in dry fields where prey has been concentrated or disturbed.
value.behavior: It is usually solitary or found in pairs during breeding, but may gather in flocks outside the breeding season and sometimes joins other wading birds. Individuals walk slowly through shallow water and may compete for concentrated prey, including occasional food stealing among storks. The species is primarily diurnal and adapted to open landscapes. Its ground-level nesting and defensive behavior by chicks are unusual among storks and reflect the risks of nesting in exposed wetlands.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable, although precise population estimates and movement patterns remain limited.
